Given an element $a$ in a semigroup $S$, the following statements are equivalent.
	\begin{enumerate}
		\item[(i)] $a$ has an outer inverse in $S$.
		\item[(ii)] There exists an idempotent element $e \in S$ such that $eS \subseteq aS$.
		\item[(iii)] There exists an idempotent element $f \in S$ such that $Sf \subseteq Sa$.
	\end{enumerate}
	                                                                                                                  
In fact $e = ax = ya$	for some $x,y \in T(a)$.

{\label{refinement}}
	Let $R$ be a ring and let $a \in \text{Reg}(R)$, $z \in I(a)$ and $e = az$. Then the following hold:
	\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
		\item $T(a)=\Bigl\{\bigl(z +(1-za)r\bigr)\,\,g\,w(y)\ \bigm|\ r\in R,\ g=g^{2}\in eRe\Bigr\}$
		
		\item $\text{Ref }(a)=\Bigl\{\bigl(z +(1-za)r\bigr)\,\,e\,w(y)\ \bigm|\ r \in R\Bigr\}$
		
	\end{enumerate}
	Here $w(y)=1+ey(1-e) \qquad (x,y\in R).$

title: Proof
body_md:
$(i)$ \quad 	By Lemma 7, we have  \[T(a) = \Bigl\{\bigl(z +(1-za)r\bigr)\,v(x)\,g\,w(y)\ \bigm|\ r\in R,\ g=g^{2}\in eRe\Bigr\}\] Fixing the factor $v(x)$ to be the identity, we  have \[\Bigl\{\bigl(z +(1-za)r\bigr)\,\,g\,w(y)   \ \bigm|\ r\in R,\ g=g^{2}\in eRe\Bigr\} \subseteq T(a)\]

\noindent 	Conversely, let $x\in T(a)$.  By Lee's characterization, there exist 	$r,s,y\in R$ and an idempotent $g\in eRe$ such that
	\[	
x=\bigl(z+(1-za)r\bigr)v(s)\,g \,w(y),	
	\]
	where $v(s)=1+(1-az)s(e)$ and $	w(y)=1+azy(1-az).$ \\
	Then we can write 
	\begin{align*}
		x  &= \bigl(z+(1-za)r\bigr)\, \underbrace{(1+(1-az)s(e))}_{v(s)} \,g \,w(y) \\
		&= \bigl(z + (1-za)r + (z-zaz)se + (1-za)r(1-az)se\bigr)\,g \,w(y) \\
		&= \bigl(z + (1-za)(r +zse + r(1-az)se)\bigr)\,g \,w(y) \\
		&= \bigl(z + (1-za)r' \bigr)\,g \,w(y) \text{ for some } r' \in R\
	\end{align*}

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{outer0}
	Let $R$ be a ring, let $a$ be a von Neumann regular element of $R$, and let $x$ be an arbitrary outer inverse of $a$. Then the following hold.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item There exists a family of reflexive inverses $\{x_{r,k}\}$ of $a$ such that
		\[
		x\leq^- x_{r,k}
		\]
		for every $k$.
		\item Every member of the family,
		\[
		\{x_{r,k}-x\}
		\]
		is von Neumann regular with a common inner-inverse and
		\[
		x_{r,k}-x\leq^- x_{r,k}.
		\]
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $a = aza$ for some  $z \in R$ and let $x$ be any  outer inverse of $a$. Using the refinement in Lemma \ref{refinement}, we can write 
	\[x = \left(z  + (1-za)r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}\right) g v \hspace{2mm} \text{ for some fixed } r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} \in R \text{ and } g^2=g \in (az)R(az)\]
	where $v = 1 + (az)t(1-az)$ for some fixed $t \in R$. \\
	
	Set $x_{s,k}= \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g))\right] (az) v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}$ where $v_{\scriptscriptstyle k} = 1 + az(gt +(az-g)k)(1-az)$ for arbitrary $s,k \in R$. Clearly $v_{\scriptscriptstyle k} \in U(R).$\\
	Then $a(x_{s,k}) = (az)v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}$ and $(x_{s,k} )a = \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g))\right] a$. Then it can be easily seen that  $(x_{s,k})a(x_{s,k})=x_{s,k}$ and $a(x_{s,k})a= aza=a$. \\
	
	\noindent We prove that $x \leq^{-} x_{s,k}$. \\
	
	\noindent Take the element $ y = ga$ where $g^2=g \in (az)R(az)$ in the outer inverse $x = \left(z  + (1-za)r\right) g v_1 $.\\
	Since $vg = g = v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}g$ and $g^2=g$, we have 
	\begin{align*}
		x(ga)x = xg(ax) &= (xg )(gv)\\
		&= ( \left(z  + (1-za)r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}\right) (g vg ) (gv) \\
		&=  \left(z  + (1-za)r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}\right) g v  = x
	\end{align*}
	
	\noindent  Thus $ga$ is an inner inverse of $x$. Furthermore we have, 
	\begin{align*}
		(x_{s,k})(ga)  &= \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g))\right] (az) v_k (ga)\\
		&=  \left[ z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g))\right] (ga)\hspace{4mm} \cdots \hspace{4mm} \because (az) g = g \\
		&=  \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})\right] (ga) \\
		&= x(ga)
	\end{align*}
	and \hspace{2mm}	$(ga)(x_{s,k})  = g(a(x_{s,k}))=  g (az)v_{\scriptscriptstyle k} = g(v_{\scriptscriptstyle k})$ \hspace{1mm} where 
	                                                                        
	                        
	\begin{align*}
		g  (v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}) &= g(1 + az(gt +(az-g)k)(1-az)) \\
		&= g + g(gt +(az-g)k)(1-az)) \\
		&= g + gt (1-az) \\
		&= g (az) + g(az)^2t (1-az) \hspace{4mm} \cdots  \hspace{4mm} \because g(az) = g = g(az)^2\\
		&= g(az)(1 + (az)t(1-az)) = g(1 + (az)t(1-az)) =  gv.
	\end{align*}
	Therefore, $(ga)(x_{s,k})  = gv = g(ax) = (ga)x$ \\
	Thus,  $x \leq^{-} x_{s,k}$ \\
	\noindent $(ii)$ We now prove that each member of the family  $\{x_{s,k} -x\}$ is von Neumann regular and $(x_{s,k}-x )\leq^{-} x_{s,k}$.\\
	First, it can be seen that $a(x_{s,k} - x) = (az)v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}  - gv  $ and 
	\begin{align*}
		(x_{s,k} - x) (az - g) &= x_{s,k} (az) - (x_{s,k}) g - x(az) + xg \\
		&= \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g))\right] (az)  - \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g))\right] g  \\ & \hspace{4mm} - \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})\right] g + xg \\
		&= (x_{s,k})v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}^{-1} - \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})\right] g  \\
		\implies (x_{s,k} - x) (az - g) v_{\scriptscriptstyle k} &=  (x_{s,k}) - \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})\right] gv_{\scriptscriptstyle k}
	\end{align*}
	\begin{align*}
		\text{Therefore,  } (x_{s,k} - x) (az - g)a (x_{s,k} - x) &= (x_{s,k} - x) (az - g) a (x_{s,k} - x) )\\
		&= (x_{s,k} - x) (az - g)((az)v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}  - gv) \\
		&= (x_{s,k} - x) ((az)v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}  - gv - gv_{\scriptscriptstyle k} + gv)\\
		&= (x_{s,k} - x) (az - g) v_{\scriptscriptstyle k} \\
		&= (x_{s,k})- \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})\right] (g v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}) \\
		&= (x_{s,k})- \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})\right] (g v) \\
		&= (x_{s,k} - x)
	\end{align*}
	Thus, each member of the family  $\{x_{s,k} -x\}$ is von Neumann regular with a common inner inverse $a-ga$.
	\begin{align*}
		\text{Furthermore,  }  (az - g)a (x_{s,k} - x) &= (az - g)((az)v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}  - gv) \\ 
		&= (az - g) v_{\scriptscriptstyle k} \\ 
		&= (az - g) (az)v_{\scriptscriptstyle k} \\ 
		&= (az - g) a(x_{s,k}) \hspace{50mm}
	\end{align*}
	Now to show that $(x_{s,k} - x)  (az - g)a  = (x_{s,k} )(az - g)a  $ we first observe that since $(a-ga) = (az-g)(a-ga)$ we have 
	\begin{align*}
		(x_{s,k} )(az-g)a &=  \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g)\right] (az-g) a  \\ 
		&= \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s)\right]  (az-g) (a-ga)  \\ 
		&= \left[z  + (1-za)r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} \right](a-ga)   + \left[(1-za)s\right](az-g)(a-ga)   \\
		&=  \left[z  + (1-za)r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} \right]a -  \left[z  + (1-za)r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} \right](ga) + \\ 
		& \hspace{4mm} \left[(1-za)s\right](az - g)(a) - \underbrace{\left[(1-za)s\right](az - g)(ga) }_{0} \\
		&=  \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g)\right] a  -   \left[z  + (1-za)r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} \right](ga) 
	\end{align*}
	\begin{align*}
		\text{ where, }  (x_{s,k} - x)(az-g)a &= (x_{s,k})v_{\scriptscriptstyle k}^{-1}a - \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})\right]  ga \\ 
		&=  \left[ z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} + s(az-g)\right] (a) - \left[z  + (1-za)(r_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})\right]  ga \\ 
	\end{align*}
	Therefore, $(x_{s,k}-x )\leq^{-} x_{s,k}$ for each $s,k \in R$.

title: Corollary
body_md:
{\label{outer}}
	Let $R$ be a ring and $a \in R$. The following are equivalent. 
	\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
		\item $a$ is unit-regular
		\item  Every outer inverse  of $a$ is unit-regular. 
		\item $a$ has a unit-regular inner inverse.
	\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
$(iii) \implies (i)$ If $a$ has an inner inverse $y$ that is unit-regular,  then from \cite{lam} and  \cite{siddique1}, $a$ is unit regular. For the sake of completion, we provide an alternate proof below. \\
	Suppose $yuy = y$ for some unit $u \in U(R)$. Then $1 - uy(au^{-1})(1-uy) \in U(R)$ where 
	\begin{align*}
		1 - uyau^{-1}(1-uy) &=  1 - uya(u^{-1} - y)\\
		&= 1 - uya(1-yu)u^{-1}\\
		&= u\left (1 - ya(1-yu)\right )u^{-1}\\
		&= u\left (yu + (1-ya)(1-yu)\right )u^{-1}\\
		&= u\left (y+ (1-ya)(1-yu)u^{-1}\right )
	\end{align*}
	Therefore $y+ (1-ya)(1-yu)u^{-1}  = v \in U(R)$. Pre-multiplying both sides by $a$ gives us $ay = av$. Combined with $aya = a$ gives $a = ava$.\\
	$(i) \implies (iii)$ \emph{Straightforward}. \\
	
	\noindent 	$(i) \implies (ii)$ Let $a$ be unit-regular. Then by $(i) \Leftrightarrow (iii)$ every reflexive inverse $x_{\scriptscriptstyle r}$ is unit regular since it has $a$ has an inner inverse. \\
	Choose an arbitrary outer inverse $x \in \operatorname{T}(a)$. Then by Theorem \ref{outer0}, there exists a reflexive inverses $x_r$ of $a$ such that $x \leq^{-} x_r$ where $x_r$ is unit regular. We show that $x$ is unit-regular. \\
	Now that $x_r$ is unit-regular, we can write $x_r = e u$ for some idempotent $e^2 = e$ and $u \in U(R)$. Then $u^{-1}e$ is a reflexive inverse of $x_r$ since 
\[ x_r(u^{-1}e)x_r = eu(u^{-1}e)eu = eu = x_r \]

\[\text{and, } u^{-1}e(x_r)u^{-1}e = u^{-1}e(eu)u^{-1}e = u^{-1}e\]
Consequently, $x_r \leq^{-1} u$.\\
	By transitivity of the partial order, $x \leq^{-} x_r$ and $x_r \leq^{-} u \implies x \leq^{-} u $ for some unit $u \in U(R)$. Thus, there exists  $b \in  \operatorname{Ref}(x)$ such that $bx = bu \implies b = bxb = bub.$ Thus $x$ has an inner inverse $b$ which is unit regular, and consequently, $x$ is also unit-regular.                                                       
	
	\noindent 	$(iii) \implies (i)$ If every outer inverse  of $a$ is unit-regular, then so is every reflexive inverse of $a$ and consequently, $a$ has an inner inverses $y$ that is unit-regular.

title: Theorem
body_md:
{\label{urr}}
Let $R$ be a ring with unity and let $a \in R$ be von Neumann regular. The the following are equivalent:
	\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
		\item $a$ is unit-regular. 
	\item For every outer inverse $x \in T(a),$ there exists $s\in U(R)$ such that \[x+ (1-xa)s(1-ax) \in U(R) \] 
	\item For every reflexive inverse $x \in Ref(a)$, there exists $ t\in U(R)$ such that  \[a + (1-ax)t(1-xa)) \in U(R) \]
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(i) \implies (ii)$. Let $a$ be unit-regular. \\Choose an arbitrary outer inverse $x \in T(a)$. Then by Corollary \ref{outer}, $x$ is unit-regular and subsequently, there exists $v \in U(R)$ such that $x = xvx$. Label $e = ax, f = xa$. 
	\[\text{Set } \,\,c = (1-xa)v^{-1}(1-ax) \,\,\, \text{ and } \, d = v - vxv\]
Label	$p=xv$, $q=vx$. Then $p^2=p$, $q^2=q$, and  $d=(1-q)v=v(1-p)$. \\
In fact, we  have 
\[fp=(xax)v=xv=p \quad \text{ and } \quad  pf=(xvx)a=xa=f\]
\[eq=a(xvx)=ax=e \quad \text{ and } \quad qe=v(xax)=vx=q\]
Passing to complements and expanding similarly as above we also have  
\[(1-f)(1-p)=1-f \quad \text{ and } \quad  (1-p)(1-f)=1-p \] \[ (1-e)(1-q)=1-q \quad \text{ and } \quad  (1-q)(1-e)=1-e \]

\noindent Then using the above expansions we have
\[(1-e)d=(1-e)(1-q)v=(1-q)v=d \] and \[d(1-f)=v(1-p)(1-f)=v(1-p)=d \]
Subsequently, expanding $cd$ and $dc$ we get \\
\begin{minipage}{0.48\textwidth}
	\begin{align*}
		cd &= \left((1-f)v^{-1}(1-e) \right) \left(d\right) \\
		&=  \left((1-f)v^{-1} \right)\underbrace{(1-e)d}_{d} \\ 
		&=  \left((1-f)v^{-1} \right) v(1-p)\\
		&=(1-f)(1-p) \\
		&=1-f
	\end{align*}
\end{minipage}
\hfill
\begin{minipage}{0.48\textwidth}
	\begin{align*}
		dc &= (d)\left((1-f)v^{-1}(1-e) \right) \\
		&=  \underbrace{d(1-f)}_{d}v^{-1}(1-e)\\
		&=(1-q)v \left(v^{-1}(1-e)\right) \\
		&=(1-q)(1-e) \\
		&= 1-e\\
	\end{align*}
\end{minipage}

\noindent Then clearly, $(x+c) \in U(R)$ with inverse $axa + d,$  since  
\begin{align*}
		(axa+d)(x+c) &= (ax)(ax)   \, +  \, (axa)c  \, + \,  dx  \, + \, dc \\
		&= \underbrace{ax}_{e} + a\underbrace{(xa)c}_{0}  \, +  \, \underbrace{(v-vxv)x}_{0}  \, +  \, \underbrace{dc}_{1-e}=  1
\end{align*}
\begin{align*}
	(x+c)(axa + d) &= (xa)(xa)  \, +  \, c(axa) \, +  \, xd  \, +  \, cd \\
	&= \underbrace{xa}_{f} + \underbrace{c(ax)}_{0}a + \underbrace{x(v-vxv)}_{0} + \underbrace{cd}_{1-f}=  1
\end{align*}
Thus, $x+ (1-xa)s(1-ax) \in U(R) $ for some $s = v^{-1} \in U(R)$ where $xvx = x$.\\
               
                                                                                          
                             
                                                                          
                                      
             
                                                       
 
\noindent $(i) \implies (iii):$ Let $a$ be unit-regular. Choose an arbitrary  reflexive inverse $ x \in Ref(a)$ such that $axa = a$ and $xax = x$. Then $x$ is also unit regular  and there exists $v \in U(R)$ such that $x = xvx$. Then similarly as above, setting $e=ax, f=xa$ and $d = v-vxv$, we have $(axa +d)= a+d$ is invertible with inverse $x +c$. Since we also have  $(1-e)d = d$ and $d(1-f) = d,$ then together with $a = axa$ we get 
 \begin{align*}
 	(1-e)(a+d)(1-f) &= (1-e)a(1-f) \, + \, (1-e)d(1-f)\\
 	&= 0 \, + \,  (1-e)d(1-f) = d
 \end{align*}
Setting $t= (a+d)$ we get  $a + (1-ax)t(1-xa) \in U(R)$ for $t \in U(R)$. \\
$(ii) \implies (i):$ Let $x$ be any outer inverse of $a.$ Then by Theorem \ref{outer0}, there exists a reflexive inverse $y \in Ref(a)$ such that $x \leq^{-} y$. As $y$ is also an outer inverse of $a$,  there exists $s \in U(R)$ such that \[y + (1-ya)s(1-ay) \in U(R)\] 
whence  $a\left(y + (1-ya)s(1-ay) \right)a = aya = a.$ \\
$(iii) \implies (i):$ Choose an outer inverse $x$ of $a$. Then by Theorem \ref{outer0}  there exists a reflexive inverse $y \in Ref(a)$ such that $x \leq^{-} y$. By assumption, there exists $s \in U(R)$ such that \[a + (1-ay)s(1-ya) \in U(R)\] Then $y$ is unit-regular since $y(a + (1-ay)s(1-ya))y = y,$ and subsequently, $a$ has a unit-regular inner inverse $y$ and by Theorem \ref{outer}, $a$ is unit-regular.

title: Remark
body_md:
We draw attention to the structure of the proof of $(i)\Rightarrow(ii)$ 
	above. Recall the classical criterion of unit regularity in Ehrlich \cite{ehrlich} (see also 
	Handelman \cite{handelman}):\\
	 \emph{A regular ring R is unit-regular if and only
	if for every two idempotents, $e \sim f \implies (1-e) \sim (1-f)$.}\\
The construction $c\in(1-f)R(1-e)$ and 
$d\in(1-e)R(1-f)$ satisfying $cd=1-f$ and $dc=1-e$  yields a purely element-wise, ring-theoretic proof of the classical characterization without module-theoretic machinery.

title: Definition
body_md:
An element $a \in R$ is said to be \emph{left annihilator-stable} (or simply, a \emph{left AS element}) if  whenever $Ra + \mathrm{ann}_l(b) = R$,  there exists a unit $u \in U(R)$ such that \[a - u \in \mathrm{ann}_l(b)\] 
A ring $R$ is called a \emph{left AS ring} if every element of $R$ is left AS.

We prove that $ 	\{b : Ra + \operatorname{ann}_\ell(b) = R\} \subseteq \bigcup_{x \in T(a)} xR$.\\
Let
$Ra + \operatorname{ann}_\ell(b) = R \iff b = rab$ for some $r \in R$.  Label $a' = ra$ where $(1-a')b = 0$. Since $R$ is an exchange ring, by Nicholson's
characterization there is an idempotent $e \in Ra' \subseteq Ra$ with $1 - e \in R(1-a').$  Set idempotent $e = ra$ and  $1 - e = s(1-a')$. Then $(1-e)b = s(1-a')b = 0 \implies  eb = b $. \\
 Label $x = rar$. Then $xa  = e^2 = e$ and $xax = ex = x \implies x \in T(a)$ where
\[ x(ab) = (xa)b = eb = b   \]
Thus  $b \in xR$ for some $x \in T(a)$. \\

label: prp7
title: Corollary
body_md:
{\label{prp7}}
	For any ring $R$ the following conditions are equivalent :
	\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
		\item $R$ is partially unit-regular. 
		\item For every $a \in R$ and any outer inverse $x \in T(a)$,   there exists an invertible element $u \in U(R)$ such that $ a- u \in \operatorname{ann}_r(x) \cap \operatorname{ann}_\ell(x)$
		\item For every  $a \in R$ and any outer inverse $x \in T(a)$,   there exists an invertible element $u \in U(R)$ such that $ a- u \in \operatorname{ann}_{l}(x) \left(\text{equivalently, } \operatorname{ann}_r(x)\right)$
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(i) \implies (ii):$	Let $a\in R$ and  $x$ be an arbitrary outer inverse of $a$. Then $xax = x$. Then $x$ is von Neumann regular, with $a$ as an inner inverse, and hence $x$ is unit-regular by $(i)$. Moreover $a' = axa$ is an outer inverse of $x$, using $xax = x$, and therefore  $a' \in T(x)$. Applying Theorem~\ref{urr}$(ii)$ to the unit-regular element
$x$ and its outer inverse $a'$, there exists $s \in U(R)$ such that
\[  a' + (1-a'x)s(1-xa') = axa + (1-ax)s(1-xa) \in U(R). \]
	Label $u = axa +(1-ax)s(1-xa)$.  Since $x(1-ax) = 0$ and $(1-xa)x = 0$, we obtain
\[ xu = x(axa) = xa \qquad \text{and} \qquad ux = (axa)x = ax, \]
hence $x(a-u) = 0 = (a-u)x$, that is, $a-u \in \operatorname{ann}_r(x) \cap \operatorname{ann}_\ell(x)$.
                                                                                                                                                                                             
	                                                                                                                                               
	                                
	
	                                                                                    

                                                                                                                                                                                                       
                                                                                                               
	$(ii) \implies (i):$ 
	Let $a \in R$ be von Neumann regular and choose $x \in \mathrm{Ref}(a)$. 
	In particular, $x$ is an outer inverse of $a$, so by hypothesis there 
	exists $u \in U(R)$ with
	$$a - u \in \mathrm{ann}_\ell(x) \cap \mathrm{ann}_r(x).$$
	From $x(a-u) = 0$ and $(a-u)x= 0$ we obtain $xa = xu$ and $ax = ux$. Since  $x \in \operatorname{Ref}(a)$ we must have   $a \leq^{-} u$ where $u \in U(R).$  \\
Consequently,  $a$ is unit-regular. \\
$(ii) \iff (iii):$ Straightforward. \\
$(iii) \iff (i):$ Follows directly from \cite{siddique1} Prop. $9(iii)$. \\
Equivalently, the proof is similar if we  replace $\operatorname{ann}_{l}(x)$ with $\operatorname{ann}_{r}(x).$

body_md: A regular ring $R$ is unit-regular if and only if it is left UG.

label: outerinverse
title: Lemma
body_md:
{\label{outerinverse}}
Let $a \in R$ be von Neumann regular with $z \in \operatorname{I}(a)$, and let $x$ be
an outer inverse of $a$. Label $B_x= \{\, y \in \operatorname{T}(1-a) \;:\; ax + (1-a)y = 1 \,\}$.

Then the following are equivalent:
 \begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
 	\item $(1-ax) \in (1-a)R$
 	\item  $B_x \neq \phi$.
 \end{enumerate} 
  In this case, $B_x = \{(1-az) + r(1-ax) : r \in \operatorname{ann}_{r}(1-a) \cap R(1-ax)\}$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\noindent  Clearly for every outer inverses $x$ of $a$, $(1-ax)$ is an idempotent. \\
$(\Longrightarrow)$ Suppose $(1-ax)= (1-a)z$ for some $z\in R$. Choose $y =  z(1-ax).$ Then $y(1-ax) = y$ and $y(1-a)y = y(1-a)z(1-ax) = y(1-ax) = y.$ Thus $y \in B_x$. \\
The converse is straightforward.\\

                                                                                                      
In addition, suppose  $B  \neq \phi$  and choose arbitrary  $ y \in B$. Label 
$y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} = 1-az$. It satisfies $y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}(1-a)y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}=y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}$ since $(1-az)a = a-aza=0$. Furthermore 
\[
(1-a)y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0} = (1-a)(1-az) = (1-ax)
\]
                         
Set $k = y - y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}$. Then clearly, $(1-ax)k = (1-ax) (y-y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}) = (1-ax) -(1-ax) = 0$ and $k (ax) =  (y-y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0})ax  = 0 \implies k = k(1-ax) \in R(1-ax)$. Thus \[B \subseteq \{(1-az) + k(1-ax) : k \in \operatorname{ann}_{r}(1-ax) \cap R(1-ax)\} \]
Conversely, for any element $y_{\scriptscriptstyle k} \in \{(1-az) + k(1-ax) : r \in \operatorname{ann}_{r}(1-a) \cap R(1-ax)\} $ we clearly have
\begin{align*}
(1-a)y_{\scriptscriptstyle k} &= (1-a)\underbrace{(1-az)}_{ y_{\scriptscriptstyle 0}}+ \underbrace{(1-a)k}_{0}(1-ax) \\
&= 1-ax
\end{align*} 
and $y_{\scriptscriptstyle k}(1-a)y_{\scriptscriptstyle k}= y_{\scriptscriptstyle k} (1-ax) = y_{\scriptscriptstyle k}$. Thus \\
\[B_x= \{(1-az) + k(1-ax) : k \in \operatorname{ann}_{r}(1-a) \cap R(1-ax)\}\]

label: reflex1
title: Proposition
body_md:
{\label{reflex1}}
		Let $R$ be a ring and $a \in R$.  Then $a$ is von Neumann regular  if and only if there exists a reflexive $($outer$)$  inverse $x$ of $a$ and outer inverse $y$ of $(1-a)$ such that the following hold.
	\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
		\item $ax +(1-a)y = 1$
		\item $a(x-y)a = a$
	\end{enumerate}
	Additonally, if $(x-y)$ is invertible then $a$ is clean (and unit-regular).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(\Longleftarrow): Straightforward$ \\
		$(\Longrightarrow):$ 
	Let $a$ be von Neumann regular. Choose  $z$ to be an inner-inverse of $a$. Then by the Refinement Lemma \ref{refinement}, the set of all reflexive inverses of $a$ is given by 
	\[\text{Ref}(a) = \{ (z+ (1-za)r)(az)(1+ azt(1-az)): \forall r,s,t \in R\}\]
	
	\noindent 	Choose a reflexive inverse of $a.$  Then, it is of the  form 
	\[x = \left(z + (1-za)r \right) \left(az\right)\left(1+azt(1-az)\right) \text{ for some } r,t \in R\]
	\noindent Then, $ax = az\left(az + azt(1-az)\right) = az + azt(1-az)$ for some $t\in R$. \\
	
\noindent  Furthermore, $1-ax = 1 - (az + azt(1-az)) = (1-azt)(1-az).$ Pluggin in $t = a$ gives us $1-ax = (1-a)(1-az)$. \\
\noindent 	We find $y \in R$ such that $y(1-a)y = y $ and $(1-a)y = 1 - ax.$ \\
\noindent Since $(1-ax) \in (1-a)R$, from Lemma \ref{outerinverse}, the set $B_x= \{y \in \operatorname{T}(1-a): (1-a)y + ax = 1 \}  \neq \phi,$ and therefore  we can get a family of such outer inverses  of $(1-a)$ given by \[ \{(1-az) + k(1-ax) : k \in \operatorname{ann}_{r}(1-a) \cap R(1-ax)\}\]
	
	\noindent Therefore, choosing $y_{\scriptscriptstyle k} =   (1-az) \, +  k(1-ax) \in B$  and $x_{\scriptscriptstyle r} =  x= (z + (1-za)r ) (az)(1+a(1-az))$  for any $r \in R$  satisfies 	\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
		\item $x_{\scriptscriptstyle r}ax_{\scriptscriptstyle r} = x_{\scriptscriptstyle r}$  and $ax_{\scriptscriptstyle r}a= a$
		\item $y_{\scriptscriptstyle k}(1-a)y_{\scriptscriptstyle k}=  y_{\scriptscriptstyle k}$
		\item $ax_{\scriptscriptstyle r} +(1-a)y_{\scriptscriptstyle k}= 1$\\
	\end{enumerate}
	
To prove the additional part, we use the term $(x-y)$ to characterize $a$ explicitly. 
	\noindent Set $e = ax$. Then $e^2 = e, \; x \cdot e = x,  \text{ and }y \cdot(1-e) = y. $    Then we can write, 
	\begin{align*}
		a(x-y) - (x-y)(1-e) &= ax - ay - (x-y) + (x-y)e \\
		&= (ax) + ((1-a)y )- x + xe \\
		&= (e) + (1-e)\\
		&= 1
	\end{align*}
	This is true for all values of $x=  \left(z + (1-za)r \right) \left(az\right)\left(1+a(1-az)\right) \text{ for  } r \in R$. \\
	
	\noindent Now, if $(x-y) = u$ is invertible for any  value of $r \in R,$ then we can write $a = u(1-e)u^{-1} + u^{-1}$, which shows that $a$ is clean. Additionally,\\
	
	\noindent $axa = a \implies (1-e)a = 0 \implies y(1-e)a = 0 \implies y \cdot a = 0$. Consequently, $aua = a(x-y)a = axa = a.$

label: suitable
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{suitable}
	Let $R$ be a ring and $a \in R$.  Then the following hold:
	\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
		\item $a$ is suitable
		\item There exists outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a)$ such that $ax + (1-a)y = 1$
		\item There exists outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a)$ such that  
		\[a(x-y) - (x-y)(1-e) = 1\]
		\item $(1-a)$ is suitable.
	\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(i) \implies (ii):$ Let $a$ be suitable. Then there exists an  idempotent $e \in aR$ and $(1-e) \in (1-a)R$ as per Nicholson's criterion.\\ Set $x, y \in R$ such that $ e = ax$ and $(1-e) = (1-a)y,$ which subsequently gives us $ax +(1-a)y = e+ (1-e) =1$.  We can choose $x,y \in R$ such that $xax = x$ and $y(1-a)y= y,$ for otherwise  set $x' = xax$. Then $x'ax' = x'$ and $ax' = ax \implies (1-a)y +ax' = 1$. \\
$(ii) \implies (i):$ Choose $x,y \in R$ such that $xax = x, y(1-a)y = y$ and $ax + (1-a)y = 1$. Set $e = ax$ and $f = (1-a)y$. Then $f = 1-e$ where $e \in aR$ and $f = 1-e \in (1-a)R$.\\
$(i) \implies (iii):$ 	 Let $a$ be suitable. Then there exists an idempotent $e^2 = e \in E(R)$ such that $e = ar$ and $1-e = (1-a)s$. Choose $r,s$ such that $re = r$ and $s(1-e)=s$. \\
Then $rar= r, s(1-a)s = s$ and 
\begin{align*}
	a(r-s) - (r-s)(1-e) &=	a(r-s) + s(1-e) \\
	&= ar - as + s \\
	&= ar + (1-a)s\\ 
	&= e + (1-e) =1
\end{align*}
$(iii) \implies (i)$ Let there exists $x,y \in R $ such that \[a(x-y) -  (x-y)f = 1 \] for some $f = f^2 \in R$. Post-multiplying by $(1-f)$ and $f$ respectively, we get
\[a(x-y)(1-f) = (1-f)  \hspace{3mm} \text{ and } \hspace{3mm} (1-a)(y-x)f = f  \]
Thus $a$ is exchange.\\
Finally, $(i)\Longleftrightarrow(iv)$ follows from the symmetry of Nicholson’s criterion.

title: Remark
body_md: An equivalent criterion $(x-y)a-(1-e)(x-y)=1$ for suitability of elements can be obtained by using idempotents in $Ra$ and $R(1-a)$.

title: Corollary
body_md: Let $R$ be a ring and $a \in R$.  Then $a$ is clean if and only if there exists outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a)$ such that $ax + (1-a)y = 1$ and  $(x-y)$ is invertible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(\Longleftarrow)$	If there exists outer inverse $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a)$ such that  $ax + (1-a)y = 1$ then by Theorem \ref{suitable} we can write 
		\[a(x-y) - (x-y)(1-e) = 1\] 
		Since $(x-y)$ is invertible, setting $u = x-y$  we can write $a = u(1-e)u^{-1} + u^{-1}$, which shows that $a$ is clean. \\
		
			$\Longrightarrow$ Let $a$ be clean. Then there exists an idempotent $f^2 = f \in R$ and unit $u \in U(R)$ such that
			\[a = f + u^{-1}\]
			Set $(1-e) = u^{-1}fu$. Then, $ f = u(1-e)u^{-1}$ and we can write \[a = u(1-e)u^{-1} + u^{-1} \hspace{5mm} \cdots \hspace{5mm} eq.(i)\]
			Set $ x = ue$ and $y = (-u)(1-e)$. Then, we can see that $x - y = u \in U(R)$.\\
			Infact, $xax = ue\left(u(1-e)u^{-1} + u^{-1}\right) ue = ue = x$. \\
			Now rerranging terms in $eq.(i)$ we  see that
			\begin{align*}
				1-a &= 1- \left(u(1-e)u^{-1} + u^{-1} \right) \\
				&= ueu^{-1} - u^{-1}
			\end{align*}
			Then, $y(1-a)y = (-u)(1-e)\left(ueu^{-1} - u^{-1}\right)(-u)(1-e)= (-u)(1-e) =y$
			\begin{align*}
				\text{Furthermore, } ax + (1-a)y &= \left(u(1-e)u^{-1} + u^{-1}\right)(ue) + \left(ueu^{-1} - u^{-1}\right)(-u)(1-e)\\
				&= e + (1-e) = 1
			\end{align*}
			Hence, there exists outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a)$ such that $(x-y)$ is invertible and  $ax + (1-a)y = 1$.\\
			Additionally, from $eq.(i)$ we can also write \[a (x-y) - (x-y)(1-e) = 1\]

title: Proposition
body_md:
Let $R$ be a ring. Then the following are equivalent 
	\begin{enumerate}[label = (\roman*)]
		\item $a$ is unit-exchange.
		\item There exists  outer inverses $r,s$ of $ua$ and $1-ua$ respectively, such that 
		\[(r-s)ua- f(r-s)= 1\]
		for some idempotent $f \in R$ 
				\item For some $u \in U(R)$, there exists  outer inverses $r,s$ of $au$ and $1-au$ respectively, such that 
		\[au(r-s) - (r-s)f = 1\]
		for some idempotent $f \in R$ 
		\item $(1-a)$ is unit-exchange
	\end{enumerate}	
	Additionally $a$ is unit clean if and only if $(r-s)$ is invertible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
$(i) \implies (ii)$ The proof follows similarly as in the case of suitable rings above in Theorem \ref{suitable}. \\                                                                                                                                                                                               
	                                  
	               
	                                             
	                      
	                     
	                
	     
	             
	$(ii) \implies (i)$ Conversely, let there exists $r,s \in R $ such that $au(r-s) -  (r-s)f = 1 $ for some $f = f^2 \in R$ and for some $u\in U(R).$  \\
	
Multiplying this identity on the left by $1-f$, we obtain
\[(1-f)(r-s)ua=1-f.\]
Define  $\gamma=(1-f)(r-s)u.$
Then $\gamma a=1-f \implies 1-\gamma a=f.$ Moreover, $\gamma$  is an outer inverse of $a$, since
\begin{align*}
\gamma a\gamma
&=(1-f)(r-s)u\,a(1-f)(r-s)u \\
&=(1-f)(r-s)u(1-f)=\gamma.
\end{align*}


\noindent Next, multiplying
$(r-s)ua-f(r-s)=1$
on the left by $f$, we get
$f(r-s)ua-f(r-s)=f.$
Equivalently,
$f(r-s)(ua-1)=f.$
Since
$ua-1=u(a-u^{-1}),$
this gives
$f(r-s)u(a-u^{-1})=f.$
Multiplying on the right by $f$, and using $f^{2}=f$, yields
\[f(r-s)u(a-u^{-1})f=f.\]
Thus, if
$\sigma=f(r-s)u
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
v=u^{-1},$
then
\[\sigma(a-v)(1-\gamma a)=1-\gamma a.\]
	
	
	
	
                                                           
                                                                                     
\noindent 	Then by \cite{siddique1}  Proposition 20, $a$ is unit-exchange. \\
For the additional part, the solution follows similarly as above in the case of suitable rings.

label: sclean
title: Proposition
body_md:
{\label{sclean}}
	Let $a \in R.$ If there exists  outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a),$ such that $(1-a)y + ax = 1$ and  $(x-y) \in C(a),$ then $a$ is strongly clean.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $a \in R$. Choose $x,y \in R$ such that \[xax = x, \; y(1-a)y = y, \; \text{ and } ax + (1-a)y = 1\] Set $e = ax.$ Then from $ x(1-e)=0, \; y(1-e) = y, \; (1-e) = (1-a)y$  we have 
	\[a(x-y) - (x-y)(1-e) = 1\]
	Now, $x-y \in C(a) \implies  (x-y)\left(a - (1-e)\right) = 1$. \\
	On the other hand, 
	\begin{align*}
		\left(a - (1-e)\right) (x-y) &= a(x-y) - (1-e)x + (1-e)y \\
		&= \underbrace{ax +(1-a)y}_{1}  - ey - (1-e)x \\
		&= 1 - ey - (1-e)x  \hspace{35mm} \cdots \hspace{5mm}(i)\\
		                                                                         
	\end{align*}
	Since $(x-y)$ commutes with $a$ we have $(x-y)a  = a(x-y)$ where 
	\begin{align*}
		a(x-y) &= ax - ay \\
		&= e + (1-a)y - y \\
		&= 1 + (1-e) - 1 \\
		&= 1-y
	\end{align*}
	Therefore, $(x-y)a  = 1-y \implies (x-y)ax  = (1-y)x \implies yax = yx$ where $yax = y\cdot e = (y(1-e))\cdot e=0$. Therefore $yx = 0$. \\
	Then, $(1-e) = (1-a)y \implies  (1-e)x =(1-a)yx = 0 \implies x = ex$. Thus, $x = ex = xe \in eRe$.\\
	Then from \emph{eq.}$(i)$ above, since  $e(x-y)(1-e)$ is a nilpotent element we have
	\begin{align*}
		\left(a - (1-e)\right) (x-y) &= 1 - ey - (1-e)x  \\
		&= 1 + e(x-y)(1-e)  \in U(R)
	\end{align*}
	Thus, $(x-y)$ is both left and right-invertible and is therefore an unit in $R$ with \[(x-y)(a - (1-e) )= 1\]
	 Therefore  $a -(1-e) = (x-y)^{-1}$  where $(x-y)$ commutes with $a$ and hence, also with $e=ax.$ Consequently, $a$ is strongly clean. \\
	\begin{remark}
		For any $a \in R$ if there exists  outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a),$ such that $(1-a)y + ax = 1$ then from above we see that  $(x-y)$ commutes with $a \implies (x-y)$ commutes with $ax$. \\
		On the other hand, \textbf{if  $R$ is directly finite}, then  $(x-y)$ commutes with $ax$ if and only if $(x-y)$ commutes with $a$. This is because we already have \[a(x-y) - (x-y)(1-e) = 1 \] for $e = ax$. \]

	\end{remark}

title: Theorem
body_md:
A  ring $R$ is strongly-clean if and only if  there exists outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a),$ such that $(1-a)y + ax = 1$
	and $(x-y)$ commutes with $a.$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $R$ be strongly clean. Then there exists $v \in U(R)$ and idempotent $f^2 = f$ such that $ a = f + v$ and $fv = vf$. Now we will rewrite it in the form of Sylvester's equation $AX - XB = C$ for some $B,C$  \\Set $ 1-e = v^{-1}(f)v$ and $u= v^{-1} \in U(R)$. Then we have $a = u(1-e)u^{-1} + u^{-1}$ such that $ue = eu$. Now  we re-write it as \[au-u(1-e) = 1 \text { where } ue= eu  \hspace{3mm} \cdots \hspace{3mm} (i)\]
	Set $x = ue$ and $y = -u(1-e)$. Then $(x-y)=u \in U(R).$ We can also rewrite $eq.(i)$ as 
	\[au  = 1 + u(1-e) \hspace{5mm} \text{ and } \hspace{5mm} (a-1)u = 1 - ue \] 
	With the chosen values of $x$ and $y$ we have 
	\begin{align*}
		(i) \; \; xax & = ue\underbrace{(a)u}e \hspace{100mm}\\
		&= ue(1+ u(1-e))e \\
		&= ue = x
	\end{align*}
	\begin{align*}
		(ii) \; \; y(1-a)y & = (-u)(1-e)\underbrace{(1-a)(-u)}(1-e) \hspace{100mm}\\
		&= (-u)(1-e)(1-ue)(1-e)\\
		&= (-u)(1-e) = y
	\end{align*}
	\begin{align*}
		(iii) \; \; ax +(1-a)y & = aue + (1-a)(-u)(1-e) \hspace{100mm}\\
		&= aue + (1-ue)(1-e)\\
		&= e + (1-e) = 1
	\end{align*}
	Additionally, since $ue = (x-y)e = e(x-y)$ where $u= (x-y) \in U(R)$ we see that 
	\[\left(a- (1-e)\right)(x-y) = 1 \; \;  \Longleftrightarrow \; \; (x-y)\left(a-(1-e)\right)= 1\]
	and consequently, $(x-y)$ commutes with $e = aue = ax$  $\Longleftrightarrow (x-y)$  commutes $a$.\\
	The converse follows from Proposition \ref{sclean}.

title: Corollary
body_md: An element $a \in R$ is strongly clean if and only if there exists outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a)$   such that $ax +(1-a)y = 1 \,\,( \text{or } xa + y(1-a)=1)$ and $x,y \in C(a).$

title: Proof
body_md:
If $x,y \in C(a)$ then $(x-y) \in C(a)$ and the proof follows from Theorem 37.\\
 On the other hand, if there exists outer inverses $x$ of $a$ and $y$ of $(1-a)$ such that $(x-y)\in C(a)$ then $(x-y)$ is invertible, and $a$ is strongly clean where  \[a-(1-e) = (x-y)^{-1}  \]
  Now from the earlier remark, $(x-y)$ also  commutes with $e=ax$. Therefore, $xy = yx = 0 \implies x \in C(x-y) \implies x \in C(\left(x-y\right)^{-1})$.\\
 Then using $a-(1-e) = (x-y)^{-1}$  we observe that  \[ \implies x\left(a-(1-e)\right) = \left(a-(1-e)\right)x \implies ax = xa \]
Similarly, we also obtain $y \in C(a)$.\\
